When solving the equation below with standard algebraic methods, two possible solutions are found.

\[5+\sqrt{5x+94}=-x+3\]

Let \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) represent the two possible solutions, such that \(x_1<x_2\). Find both possible solutions and determine whether each is valid or extraneous.

  • \(x_1=\)
  • \(x_1\) is solution.
  • \(x_2=\)
  • \(x_2\) is solution.

\[5+\sqrt{5x+94}=-x+3\]

Subtract 5 from both sides of the equation. \[\sqrt{5x+94}=-x-2\] Square both sides of the equation. Remember, you'll need to FOIL the right side. \[5x+94=x^2+4x+4\] Subtract \(( 5x+94 )\) from both sides. \[0=x^2-x-90\] From here, you can either factor or use quadratic formula. It is easy enough to factor this one. \[0=(x+9)(x-10)\] Use the zero-product property to identify the possible solutions are \(x_1=-9\) and \(x_2=10\). Notice we correctly ordered them such that \(x_1<x_2\). Now we check which solution is valid by plugging both into the original equation.

Start with possible solution \(x=-9\) \[5+\sqrt{5(-9)+94}\stackrel{?}{=}-(-9)+3\]

\[5+\sqrt{-45+94}\stackrel{?}{=}9+3\]

\[5+\sqrt{49}\stackrel{?}{=}12\]

\[5+7\stackrel{?}{=}12\]

\[12=12\] So we see \(x=-9\) is a valid solution.

Now check possible solution \(x=10\) \[5+\sqrt{5(10)+94}\stackrel{?}{=}-(10)+3\]

\[5+\sqrt{50+94}\stackrel{?}{=}-10+3\]

\[5+\sqrt{144}\stackrel{?}{=}-7\]

\[5+12\stackrel{?}{=}-7\]

\[17\ne -7\] So we see \(x=10\) is an extraneous solution.

When solving the equation below with standard algebraic methods, two possible solutions are found.

\[-6-\sqrt{-9x-23}=-x-7\]

Let \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) represent the two possible solutions, such that \(x_1<x_2\). Find both possible solutions and determine whether each is valid or extraneous.

  • \(x_1=\)
  • \(x_1\) is solution.
  • \(x_2=\)
  • \(x_2\) is solution.

\[-6-\sqrt{-9x-23}=-x-7\]

Add 6 to both sides of the equation. \[-\sqrt{-9x-23}=-x-1\] Multiply both sides by \(-1\). \[\sqrt{-9x-23}=x+1\] Square both sides of the equation. Remember, you'll need to FOIL the right side. \[-9x-23=x^2+2x+1\] Subtract \(( -9x-23 )\) from both sides. \[0=x^2+11x+24\] From here, you can either factor or use quadratic formula. It is easy enough to factor this one. \[0=(x+8)(x+3)\] Use the zero-product property to identify the possible solutions are \(x_1=-8\) and \(x_2=-3\). Notice we correctly ordered them such that \(x_1<x_2\). Now we check which solution is valid by plugging both into the original equation.

Start with possible solution \(x=-8\) \[-6-\sqrt{-9(-8)-23}\stackrel{?}{=}-(-8)-7\]

\[-6-\sqrt{72-23}\stackrel{?}{=}8-7\]

\[-6-\sqrt{49}\stackrel{?}{=}1\]

\[-6-7\stackrel{?}{=}1\]

\[-13\ne 1\] So we see \(x=-8\) is an extraneous solution.

Now check possible solution \(x=-3\) \[-6-\sqrt{-9(-3)-23}\stackrel{?}{=}-(-3)-7\]

\[-6-\sqrt{27-23}\stackrel{?}{=}3-7\]

\[-6-\sqrt{4}\stackrel{?}{=}-4\]

\[-6-2\stackrel{?}{=}-4\]

\[-8\ne -4\] So we see \(x=-3\) is an extraneous solution.

When solving the equation below with standard algebraic methods, two possible solutions are found.

\[7+\sqrt{-5x+34}=x-1\]

Let \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) represent the two possible solutions, such that \(x_1<x_2\). Find both possible solutions and determine whether each is valid or extraneous.

  • \(x_1=\)
  • \(x_1\) is solution.
  • \(x_2=\)
  • \(x_2\) is solution.

\[7+\sqrt{-5x+34}=x-1\]

Subtract 7 from both sides of the equation. \[\sqrt{-5x+34}=x-8\] Square both sides of the equation. Remember, you'll need to FOIL the right side. \[-5x+34=x^2-16x+64\] Subtract \(( -5x+34 )\) from both sides. \[0=x^2-11x+30\] From here, you can either factor or use quadratic formula. It is easy enough to factor this one. \[0=(x-5)(x-6)\] Use the zero-product property to identify the possible solutions are \(x_1=5\) and \(x_2=6\). Notice we correctly ordered them such that \(x_1<x_2\). Now we check which solution is valid by plugging both into the original equation.

Start with possible solution \(x=5\) \[7+\sqrt{-5(5)+34}\stackrel{?}{=}(5)-1\]

\[7+\sqrt{-25+34}\stackrel{?}{=}5-1\]

\[7+\sqrt{9}\stackrel{?}{=}4\]

\[7+3\stackrel{?}{=}4\]

\[10\ne 4\] So we see \(x=5\) is an extraneous solution.

Now check possible solution \(x=6\) \[7+\sqrt{-5(6)+34}\stackrel{?}{=}(6)-1\]

\[7+\sqrt{-30+34}\stackrel{?}{=}6-1\]

\[7+\sqrt{4}\stackrel{?}{=}5\]

\[7+2\stackrel{?}{=}5\]

\[9\ne 5\] So we see \(x=6\) is an extraneous solution.

When solving the equation below with standard algebraic methods, two possible solutions are found.

  • \(x_1=\)
  • \(x_1\) is solution.
  • \(x_2=\)
  • \(x_2\) is solution.

\[9+\sqrt{6x+33}=x+10\]

Subtract 9 from both sides of the equation. \[\sqrt{6x+33}=x+1\] Square both sides of the equation. Remember, you'll need to FOIL the right side. \[6x+33=x^2+2x+1\] Subtract \(( 6x+33 )\) from both sides. \[0=x^2-4x-32\] From here, you can either factor or use quadratic formula. It is easy enough to factor this one. \[0=(x+4)(x-8)\] Use the zero-product property to identify the possible solutions are \(x_1=-4\) and \(x_2=8\). Notice we correctly ordered them such that \(x_1<x_2\). Now we check which solution is valid by plugging both into the original equation.

Start with possible solution \(x=-4\) \[9+\sqrt{6(-4)+33}\stackrel{?}{=}(-4)+10\]

\[9+\sqrt{-24+33}\stackrel{?}{=}-4+10\]

\[9+\sqrt{9}\stackrel{?}{=}6\]

\[9+3\stackrel{?}{=}6\]

\[12\ne 6\] So we see \(x=-4\) is an extraneous solution.

Now check possible solution \(x=8\) \[9+\sqrt{6(8)+33}\stackrel{?}{=}(8)+10\]

\[9+\sqrt{48+33}\stackrel{?}{=}8+10\]

\[9+\sqrt{81}\stackrel{?}{=}18\]

\[9+9\stackrel{?}{=}18\]

\[18=18\] So we see \(x=8\) is a valid solution.

When solving the equation below with standard algebraic methods, two possible solutions are found.

\[-2+\sqrt{7x+44}=x+6\]

Let \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) represent the two possible solutions, such that \(x_1<x_2\). Find both possible solutions and determine whether each is valid or extraneous.

  • \(x_1=\)
  • \(x_1\) is solution.
  • \(x_2=\)
  • \(x_2\) is solution.

\[-2+\sqrt{7x+44}=x+6\]

Add 2 to both sides of the equation. \[\sqrt{7x+44}=x+8\] Square both sides of the equation. Remember, you'll need to FOIL the right side. \[7x+44=x^2+16x+64\] Subtract \(( 7x+44 )\) from both sides. \[0=x^2+9x+20\] From here, you can either factor or use quadratic formula. It is easy enough to factor this one. \[0=(x+5)(x+4)\] Use the zero-product property to identify the possible solutions are \(x_1=-5\) and \(x_2=-4\). Notice we correctly ordered them such that \(x_1<x_2\). Now we check which solution is valid by plugging both into the original equation.

Start with possible solution \(x=-5\) \[-2+\sqrt{7(-5)+44}\stackrel{?}{=}(-5)+6\]

\[-2+\sqrt{-35+44}\stackrel{?}{=}-5+6\]

\[-2+\sqrt{9}\stackrel{?}{=}1\]

\[-2+3\stackrel{?}{=}1\]

\[1=1\] So we see \(x=-5\) is a valid solution.

Now check possible solution \(x=-4\) \[-2+\sqrt{7(-4)+44}\stackrel{?}{=}(-4)+6\]

\[-2+\sqrt{-28+44}\stackrel{?}{=}-4+6\]

\[-2+\sqrt{16}\stackrel{?}{=}2\]

\[-2+4\stackrel{?}{=}2\]

\[2=2\] So we see \(x=-4\) is a valid solution.

When solving the equation below with standard algebraic methods, two possible solutions are found.

\[1+\sqrt{3x+13}=x+4\]

Let \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) represent the two possible solutions, such that \(x_1<x_2\). Find both possible solutions and determine whether each is valid or extraneous.

  • \(x_1=\)
  • \(x_1\) is solution.
  • \(x_2=\)
  • \(x_2\) is solution.

\[1+\sqrt{3x+13}=x+4\]

Subtract 1 from both sides of the equation. \[\sqrt{3x+13}=x+3\] Square both sides of the equation. Remember, you'll need to FOIL the right side. \[3x+13=x^2+6x+9\] Subtract \(( 3x+13 )\) from both sides. \[0=x^2+3x-4\] From here, you can either factor or use quadratic formula. It is easy enough to factor this one. \[0=(x+4)(x-1)\] Use the zero-product property to identify the possible solutions are \(x_1=-4\) and \(x_2=1\). Notice we correctly ordered them such that \(x_1<x_2\). Now we check which solution is valid by plugging both into the original equation.

Start with possible solution \(x=-4\) \[1+\sqrt{3(-4)+13}\stackrel{?}{=}(-4)+4\]

\[1+\sqrt{-12+13}\stackrel{?}{=}-4+4\]

\[1+\sqrt{1}\stackrel{?}{=}0\]

\[1+1\stackrel{?}{=}0\]

\[2\ne 0\] So we see \(x=-4\) is an extraneous solution.

Now check possible solution \(x=1\) \[1+\sqrt{3(1)+13}\stackrel{?}{=}(1)+4\]

\[1+\sqrt{3+13}\stackrel{?}{=}1+4\]

\[1+\sqrt{16}\stackrel{?}{=}5\]

\[1+4\stackrel{?}{=}5\]

\[5=5\] So we see \(x=1\) is a valid solution.

\[-4+\sqrt{-9x+31}=x-5\]

Add 4 to both sides of the equation. \[\sqrt{-9x+31}=x-1\] Square both sides of the equation. Remember, you'll need to FOIL the right side. \[-9x+31=x^2-2x+1\] Subtract \(( -9x+31 )\) from both sides. \[0=x^2+7x-30\] From here, you can either factor or use quadratic formula. It is easy enough to factor this one. \[0=(x+10)(x-3)\] Use the zero-product property to identify the possible solutions are \(x_1=-10\) and \(x_2=3\). Notice we correctly ordered them such that \(x_1<x_2\). Now we check which solution is valid by plugging both into the original equation.

Start with possible solution \(x=-10\) \[-4+\sqrt{-9(-10)+31}\stackrel{?}{=}(-10)-5\]

\[-4+\sqrt{90+31}\stackrel{?}{=}-10-5\]

\[-4+\sqrt{121}\stackrel{?}{=}-15\]

\[-4+11\stackrel{?}{=}-15\]

\[7\ne -15\] So we see \(x=-10\) is an extraneous solution.

Now check possible solution \(x=3\) \[-4+\sqrt{-9(3)+31}\stackrel{?}{=}(3)-5\]

\[-4+\sqrt{-27+31}\stackrel{?}{=}3-5\]

\[-4+\sqrt{4}\stackrel{?}{=}-2\]

\[-4+2\stackrel{?}{=}-2\]

\[-2=-2\] So we see \(x=3\) is a valid solution.

  • \(x_1=\)
  • \(x_1\) is solution.

\[-6-\sqrt{-9x+10}=-x-4\]

Add 6 to both sides of the equation. \[-\sqrt{-9x+10}=-x+2\] Multiply both sides by \(-1\). \[\sqrt{-9x+10}=x-2\] Square both sides of the equation. Remember, you'll need to FOIL the right side. \[-9x+10=x^2-4x+4\] Subtract \(( -9x+10 )\) from both sides. \[0=x^2+5x-6\] From here, you can either factor or use quadratic formula. It is easy enough to factor this one. \[0=(x+6)(x-1)\] Use the zero-product property to identify the possible solutions are \(x_1=-6\) and \(x_2=1\). Notice we correctly ordered them such that \(x_1<x_2\). Now we check which solution is valid by plugging both into the original equation.

Start with possible solution \(x=-6\) \[-6-\sqrt{-9(-6)+10}\stackrel{?}{=}-(-6)-4\]

\[-6-\sqrt{54+10}\stackrel{?}{=}6-4\]

\[-6-\sqrt{64}\stackrel{?}{=}2\]

\[-6-8\stackrel{?}{=}2\]

\[-14\ne 2\] So we see \(x=-6\) is an extraneous solution.

\[-6-\sqrt{1}\stackrel{?}{=}-5\]

Let \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) represent the two possible solutions, such that \(x_1<x_2\). Find both possible solutions and determine whether each is valid or extraneous.

  • \(x_1=\)
  • \(x_1\) is solution.
  • \(x_2=\)

\[5-\sqrt{-7x+50}=-x+13\]

Subtract 5 from both sides of the equation. \[-\sqrt{-7x+50}=-x+8\] Multiply both sides by \(-1\). \[\sqrt{-7x+50}=x-8\] Square both sides of the equation. Remember, you'll need to FOIL the right side. \[-7x+50=x^2-16x+64\] Subtract \(( -7x+50 )\) from both sides. \[0=x^2-9x+14\] From here, you can either factor or use quadratic formula. It is easy enough to factor this one. \[0=(x-2)(x-7)\] Use the zero-product property to identify the possible solutions are \(x_1=2\) and \(x_2=7\). Notice we correctly ordered them such that \(x_1<x_2\). Now we check which solution is valid by plugging both into the original equation.

Start with possible solution \(x=2\) \[5-\sqrt{-7(2)+50}\stackrel{?}{=}-(2)+13\]

\[5-\sqrt{-14+50}\stackrel{?}{=}-2+13\]

\[5-\sqrt{36}\stackrel{?}{=}11\]

\[5-6\stackrel{?}{=}11\]

\[-1\ne 11\] So we see \(x=2\) is an extraneous solution.

Now check possible solution \(x=7\) \[5-\sqrt{-7(7)+50}\stackrel{?}{=}-(7)+13\]

\[5-\sqrt{-49+50}\stackrel{?}{=}-7+13\]

\[5-\sqrt{1}\stackrel{?}{=}6\]

\[5-1\stackrel{?}{=}6\]

\[4\ne 6\] So we see \(x=7\) is an extraneous solution.

The equation below has one extraneous solution and one valid solution.

\[3+2\sqrt{2x+43}~=~2x+11\]

We can find both using Desmos. To find the valid solution, find the intersection of the following two curves:

\[f(x)=3+2\sqrt{2x+43}\] \[L(x)=2x+11\]

You should see half a parabola facing sideways and a line. Click where the two curves cross. The \(x\) value is the valid solution.

The extraneous solution also has a geometric interpretation! We need to complete the parabola by plotting the following curve:

\[g(x)=3-2\sqrt{2x+43}\]

You should see the line crosses this second half of the parabola. Click on the intersection. The \(x\) value is the extraneous solution.

A transformed square-root function, \(f(x)\), and line, \(L(x)\), are parameterized and graphed below.

\[f(x)=a\sqrt{n(x-h)}+k\]

\[L(x)=mx+b\] The parameters: \[\begin{aligned} a &= \text{vertical flip and stretch} \\ n &= \text{horizontal flip and stretch} \\ h &= \text{horizontal translation} \\ k &= \text{vertical translation} \\ m &= \text{slope} \\ b &= \text{y-intercept} \end{aligned}\]
